questions_asked: At a busy US airport, which causes the longest security lines: not enough open screening lanes, or each passenger taking a long time to sort belongings into bins?
Do officers typically open an extra screening lane when the line gets very long, or do they try to speed up the passengers in each open lane first?
How many regular screening lanes does a very busy US airport typically have open at peak hours?
At the screening belt, how often do bags get flagged for a second manual search that sends the passenger to a side room?
How long does a pat-down after a metal detector alarm usually take, start to finish?
About what fraction of travelers through a US airport checkpoint hold Pre-Check at a typical day?
Does the number of people arriving at a checkpoint swing a lot between morning rush and midday, and roughly how big is the swing?
Do checkpoint lines usually start to grow again in the late-afternoon departure wave, similar to the morning rush?
How often does a single officer get briefly overwhelmed by many arrivals at once, for example after a large group boards out of an arriving gate?
Do travelers in a crowded checkpoint line mostly keep a steady order and wait, or do people frequently step around to change lanes?
expert_answers:
Not enough open screening lanes.

In practice, lane availability is the dominant driver of long lines at busy US airports. Checkpoint throughput is roughly the number of open lanes times the per-lane service rate, and the TSA's own experience (e.g., O'Hare in 2016) showed that lines collapsed when lanes were understaffed and recovered mainly by opening more lanes and adding officers. Per-passenger bin-sorting time is a real but secondary factor: it adds seconds per passenger and is partly absorbed by parallel lanes, whereas a closed lane removes an entire service channel and queues grow nonlinearly as utilization approaches 1.

The exception: if nearly all lanes are already open, then per-passenger processing time (bin sorting, divesting, pat-downs) becomes the binding constraint. But at a busy airport under normal staffing pressure, lane count is the primary bottleneck.

Officers typically open an extra lane first.

Standard practice at US checkpoints is to flex staffing to lane count: when queues build, supervisors pull officers from other posts (or call in reserves) to open additional lanes, because adding a service channel relieves the queue far more than incremental speed-ups. Speeding up passengers in existing lanes — urging them to divest faster, pre-loading bins, "please have your ID ready" — is a secondary, low-cost measure used when no additional lane or officer is available, or when all lanes are already open. So the order is: open lanes if staffing permits; otherwise push per-passenger pace.

Roughly 10–20 regular lanes open at peak at a very busy US airport (e.g., a large hub terminal), with the largest checkpoints sometimes reaching ~20–30 across all lanes including Pre-Check. This is an empirical judgment, not a precise figure; exact counts vary by terminal, checkpoint, and time of day.

Roughly 1–3% of bags get flagged for secondary manual search at the X-ray belt under normal conditions — an empirical order-of-magnitude judgment, not a precise figure. Most of those are resolved at the belt itself (bag opened, item swabbed, passenger cleared in under a minute). Only a small fraction of flagged bags — on the order of a few percent of the flagged ones, i.e. well under 1% of all passengers — escalate to a separate side room or secondary screening area. Rates rise with threat level, random/selectee screening quotas, and specific item alarms (liquids, electronics, powders).

Roughly 1–3 minutes for a routine pat-down at the checkpoint, start to finish — an empirical order-of-magnitude judgment, not a precise figure. A standard pat-down of the torso, arms, and legs takes on the order of a minute; it runs longer (3–5 minutes or more) if it escalates to a private screening area, requires removing outer layers, involves a bag search alongside, or the passenger is selected for additional screening.

About 45% of passengers at a typical US airport checkpoint are Pre-Check enrollees — that figure is given directly in the problem statement. In practice this varies by airport and time of day, but ~40–50% is a reasonable order-of-magnitude range for a typical day.

Yes, arrivals swing substantially between morning rush and midday.

At a busy US airport, the morning peak (roughly 5:00–8:00 a.m.) typically carries on the order of 2–4 times the passenger arrival rate of the midday lull (roughly 10:00 a.m.–2:00 p.m.). The swing is driven by the banked flight schedule: airlines cluster departures into waves, so checkpoints see sharp surges when a departure bank opens and troughs between banks. A ratio of about 2:1 to 4:1 peak-to-midday is a reasonable empirical order-of-magnitude judgment, not a precise figure; the exact factor varies by airport, terminal, day of week, and season, and can be larger at hubs with strongly banked schedules.

Yes, typically.

At busy US airports the late-afternoon/early-evening period (roughly 3:00–7:00 p.m.) is a second departure bank, and checkpoint queues usually build again much as they do in the morning rush. The afternoon wave is often somewhat broader and less sharply peaked than the early-morning one, and it can be comparable in magnitude or a bit lower, but the same mechanism applies: clustered departures drive a surge in arrivals that outpaces lane throughput.

This is an empirical judgment, not a precise figure; the exact size and timing vary by airport, terminal, day of week, and season, and hubs with strongly banked schedules show the effect most clearly.

Occasionally, but not as a routine steady-state condition.

At a checkpoint, arrivals are largely individual passengers released from the terminal, so a single officer rarely faces a true simultaneous "group dump." The realistic version is a short burst: a bank of flights lands or a train/shuttle disgorges, and a cluster of 10–30 passengers reaches the ID-check station within a minute or two. That can momentarily overwhelm one officer, but it is absorbed quickly because the queue simply backs up and the officer works through it at a steady rate.

Frequency: on the order of a few times per hour at a busy checkpoint during peak banks, and rarely during lulls. It is a transient queueing spike, not a sustained overload — unless staffing is already thin, in which case the spike propagates downstream. This is an empirical judgment, not a precise figure.

Mostly keep a steady order and wait.

In a crowded US checkpoint line, passengers overwhelmingly stay in their place and shuffle forward; the social norm against "cutting" and respect for personal space (noted in the problem) strongly discourages lane-switching. People do change lanes occasionally — when a neighboring lane visibly moves faster, when directed by an officer, or when a lane opens/closes — but this is the exception, not routine behavior.

The practical consequence for modeling: treat the queue as essentially first-come-first-served with stable order, and treat lane-switching as a minor, low-rate perturbation rather than a dominant dynamic. The main real exception is when an officer redirects passengers to a newly opened lane, which is a deliberate rebalancing, not spontaneous jockeying.
